newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Naples worries crime wave will ruin newfound image.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Naples worries crime wave will ruin newfound image.

text.p: When Naples Mayor Antonio Bassolino was elected four years ago, he pledged to clean up what had become a decrepit city beset by crime and corruption.
In many ways he did.
Since 1994, buildings have been refurbished, traffic reduced, and public services spruced up in a face-lift that has given this vibrant Mediterranean port a 15 percent boost in tourism.

But an upsurge of gang violence this year that has forced the Italian government to send 500 armed soldiers onto Naples' streets has left many wondering whether the much-touted revival is merely cosmetic.

"On the outside, Naples has become a shining star. But on the inside it's still rotting," said Patrizia, a 35-year-old housewife who last month saw three people shot in a gunfight between warring clans of the Camorra, the Neapolitan mafia.
SEAMY UNDERWORLD HAS ALWAYS EXISTED
Residents say the violence in which 85 people have died in the last six months is just a sign of the seamy underworld that has been there all along.
"Finally the veil that had been hung has dropped, and people are seeing that Naples has never stopped being an extremely difficult place," said anti-mob prosecutor Luigi Bobbio.
"Naples has not fallen once again into decay. It never got out. There was just a lid on it."
The Camorra, which in the last 50 years has fed off lucrative building booms and corrupt administrators, still plagues the city, prosecutors say.
While thousands of gangsters are behind bars, 80 clans still operate around Naples, with 2,000 suspected mobsters at large.
Petty crime, such as pickpocketing and purse-snatching on motor scooters, is also a continuing menace.
Police admit that only one or two of every 40 small-time crooks they catch actually stay in jail. Many are minors who are generously protected under the law, they add.
"People can't stand it anymore," said Enzo Di Leva, the owner of a cafe in the city's historic centre.
"Police catch a thief who bowls over an old lady to steal her purse, and the next day I see him out there again."
TROOPS NOT A SOLUTION
The 500 soldiers being stationed as guards around Naples at least until the end of the year are meant to allow some 350 police officers to focus on fighting organised crime.
Residents say their presence will make people feel safer, but it is by no means a solution to the city's root problem -- chronic unemployment that fuels widespread delinquency.
"The army can provide visibility for the state in a particular period, but that's it. The real solution is employment," said union leader Sergio D'Antoni.
Naples is still one of the poorest cities in Europe, with unemployment close to 25 percent, twice the national rate and higher than the average for Italy's less developed south.
"Tourism brings richness, but it doesn't bring work. Little is being done for the unemployed," said Emiddio Cozzi, 67, a retired metal worker and an activist for jobless people.
"The Camorra is successful because it is able to take advantage of the desperation of the people. Good young people go on the streets and become vandals, robbers."
A few blocks away from the splendour of Naples' gleaming waterfront, speckled with rich hotels and pleasant cafes, the dangerous alliance between crime and unemployment is palpable.
In Sanita, one of the most notorious crime-ridden districts, youths sell contraband cigarettes in garbage filled alleyways and bullet holes in the windows reveal the mark of a relentless Camorra.

"The clean-up has happened only in middle and upper-class areas. As a result, there are still no-man's-lands," Alessandra Mussolini, the far-right member of parliament and granddaughter of wartime dictator Benito Mussolini, told Reuters.
"Naples is exploding with unemployment and decay," says Mussolini, a native of the city.
MAYOR SAYS IMPROVEMENTS ARE REAL
But, with elections approaching this year, Bassolino insists that Naples' revival goes beyond the surface.
"Does this look like a city where people walk through the streets worried?" he asked, pointing to a glimmering, peaceful waterfront in the shadow of the Vesuvius volcano.

The city's revitalisation began in 1994 with a $30 million government grant that helped restore the Royal Palace, home to the 18th century Bourbon kings, and other famous landmarks before a Group of Seven summit.
Another plan to spur economic growth was the transformation of Bagnoli, once the largest industrial centre in southern Italy, into a park with hotels, restaurants and a beach.
The project is still in its preliminary stages, but officials say it will employ up to 8,000 people over 10 years and provide several thousand permanent jobs when complete.
Bassolino also said he is using some 40 billion lire ($23 million) in European Union funds to clean up Sanita and the Spanish District, another crime-ridden area.
The mayor, a former communist, admits, however, that there still are serious problems to be faced.

"The army will allow people to stroll freely through the streets of a city where people live outside more than any other in Italy," he said. "It must be accompanied by important decisions on employment and a way of life."
Many who have thrived from the revitalisation of the city worry that the army will actually harm Naples in the short run.
"It has already hurt Naples' image to have soldiers here." said Domenico Di Lecce, manager of the Jolly Hotel. "I hope we won't see a fall in tourists as a result."
One group of elderly people welcomed the soldiers with signs putting it more bluntly: "May the troops protect the tourists because they bring us money."
